title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 11–12)
hookLine: adultery, murder, and a prophet's story that makes the king see himself
carry: I have sinned against the Lord

lines: THE KING STAYS HOME FROM WAR.
A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.
A LETTER CARRIED BY ITS VICTIM.
cards: It's the turn of the year, when kings go out to war. David sends his army and stays home. One afternoon he walks on the palace roof and sees a woman bathing.
Bathsheba, Bethsabee in the Douay-Rheims, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers, away at the front. David sends for her. He's the king; nobody refuses the king.
She becomes pregnant. To hide it, David brings Uriah home, but the loyal soldier won't sleep in comfort while his comrades are in tents.
So David writes a letter, has Uriah carry it himself, and it says: put him at the front, and pull back.

teach.b: Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. Then God sends the prophet Nathan, who doesn't accuse.
He tells a story. Two men in one city. One rich, with flocks and herds.

teach.h: THE POOR MAN'S LITTLE EWE LAMB.
teach.b: One poor, with one little ewe lamb, which, the Douay says, grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and "was unto him as a daughter."
A traveler visits the rich man, who doesn't take from his own flocks. He takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David is furious.
The man who did this deserves to die! He'll pay it back four times over! And Nathan says four words: "Thou art the man."

David could see the injustice clearly as long as it was somebody else. The parable gets past his defenses, then turns around. And David, who holds all the power in the room, doesn't kill the prophet or spin it.

teach.h: I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.
teach.b: He says, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers: the Lord hath taken away thy sin. The consequences still come; the chapters ahead are full of grief in David's house.
But Nathan's word stands. Tradition gives this moment a song. The Douay's Psalm fifty, the Miserere, has a heading that sets it here, when Nathan came to David.

teach.h: THE MISERERE: HAVE MERCY ON ME.
teach.b: It begins: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy."
The Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Catholics bring its spirit into confession: say it plainly, and hear the word of pardon.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 51 (50 in the Douay numbering), the Miserere, at Morning Prayer on Fridays in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it to prepare for the sacrament of confession.

o: the soldier David sent to die at the front
the priest who anointed David as king
the prophet who told David the ewe lamb story

games.q: the king and the prophet — tap the pairs.
p: the loyal soldier sent to the front
told the story of the ewe lamb
took the poor man's only lamb
have mercy on me, O God

s: Nathan accused David directly from the start
he told a story first, and let David condemn the rich man before saying, thou art the man.
David confessed instead of punishing the prophet
Uriah carried the letter that ordered his own death
David sent it to Joab by Uriah's hand.

games.q: you're King David. a prophet has just tricked you into condemning yourself, in front of your court. you're the king. what do you do?
o: explain that kings live by different rules.
admit it: I have sinned against the Lord.
games.why: David confesses, and Nathan says the Lord has taken away his sin. the consequences still come, but the king's first move is honesty.

practice: Think of who could be your Nathan, someone who'd tell you the truth to your face, and what pattern they might name that you spot in others and not in yourself. Sit with it without arguing.
If you pray, say the Miserere's first words: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy.

wordCard.voice: Nathan. The prophet whose four words to King David turned a story about someone else into a mirror, and led the king to confess. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I have sinned. In the Hebrew, David's whole confession to Nathan is just two words.

carryVoice: Your line: I have sinned against the Lord. Said plainly, and answered with pardon. Day four hundred five, done.
